html:
A Māori haka composed around 1820 by Te Rauparaha, war leader of the Ngāti Toa tribe. It became world famous as the haka performed by New Zealand's national rugby team, the All Blacks.

The story is that during the Musket Wars, Te Rauparaha was fleeing his enemies and hid in a kūmara storage pit, with the wife of the local chief sitting over the entrance. As the hunters passed by, he chanted "Ka mate, ka mate, ka ora", "I die, I die, I live". When he climbed out into the sun, safe, he performed the haka in joy.

New Zealand rugby teams have performed it since the early 1900s, and it is the best known haka in the world. Ngāti Toa long felt their ancestor's work was used without credit, and in 2014 a law of the New Zealand Parliament recognised Te Rauparaha as its author and Ngāti Toa as its guardians. See Māori and New Zealand.
